Without a (things or unspecified people), the verb agrees with the noun: this is the pasiva refleja. Compare se busca a los responsables and se buscan camareros.
Quand le complément indirect li se combi: When the indirect object li combines with a 3rd person direct object, it takes the form hi and goes after it: el + li gives l'hi, la + li gives la hi, els + li gives els hi, les + li gives les hi. With en, you get li'n. After the verb, the pronouns are linked by hyphens.
Quand le datif li se combine avec un pro: When the dative li combines with a 3rd person direct object pronoun, li becomes hi and goes after it: el + li gives l'hi, la + li gives la hi, els + li gives els hi, les + li gives les hi. With ho and en, you get li ho and n'hi.
Quand le pronom en suit un autre pronom: When the pronoun en follows another weak pronoun before the verb, em, et, es take their full form: me'n, te'n, se'n, ens en, us en. Before a vowel or an h, en becomes n': se n'ha anat. With li, you get li'n. These combinations are very common with anar-se'n (to go away) and recordar-se'n (to remember it).
Quand le relatif dépend d'une prépositio: When the relative depends on a preposition, preposition + article + que is often used, with the usual contractions: en + a que gives na que, con + os que gives cos que. The article agrees with the antecedent. For a place, you can also say en que or onde.

Quand le verbe introducteur est au passé: When the introductory verb is in the past (dijo, explicó, contó), the tenses shift back: the present becomes imperfect, the present perfect or the preterite become pluperfect, the future becomes conditional. Time and place references change too: hoy becomes aquel día, mañana becomes al día siguiente, aquí becomes allí. If the introductory verb is in the present, the tenses don't change.

When the introductory verb is in the past (va dir, deia, havia dit), the tenses shift back: the present becomes imperfect, the future becomes conditional, the past becomes pluperfect and the imperative becomes que + imperfect subjunctive. Time and place references change too: hui becomes aquell dia, demà l'endemà, ahir el dia abans, ací allí, este aquell.
Quand le verbe principal est au conditio: When the main verb is in the conditional (me gustaría, preferiría, sería mejor), the subordinate clause in the subjunctive goes into the imperfect subjunctive, not the present. French speakers often get this wrong, because French uses the present subjunctive here. The same rule applies after a main verb in the past.
Quand le verbe principal est au passé ou: When the main verb is in the past or the conditional and requires the subjunctive, the subordinate clause goes into the imperfect subjunctive, formed on the stem of the simple past + -se (falase, comese, fixese, soubese). A trap for those who know Spanish: in Galician, the -ra form (falara) is not an imperfect subjunctive but a pluperfect indicative. So you say quería que viñeses, not quería que viñeras.

When the main verb is in the past or the conditional and requires the subjunctive, the subordinate clause goes into the imperfect subjunctive. Everyday French keeps the present (“je voulais que tu viennes”), which leads to frequent mistakes. If the main verb is in the present or the future, the present subjunctive is used.
Quand le verbe principal exprime une vol: When the main verb expresses a wish, a request, a fear or a feeling, and the subject of the subordinate clause is different, the present subjunctive is used after que. If the subject is the same, the infinitive is used.
Quand li (à lui, à elle, à vous) se comb: When li (to him, to her, to you) combines with a 3rd person direct object, li comes first: li'l, li la, li'ls, li les, li ho. Castilian se lo has no equivalent with se: “se'l” for “it to him” is wrong.
Quand on détache un complément en tête o: When a complement is dislocated to the start or end of the sentence, it must be picked up by a weak pronoun: “el, la, els, les” for a definite direct object, “en” for a complement introduced by “de” or an indefinite one, “hi” for a place or a complement with “a”. This is a very common emphatic device in Catalan.
